name: Trehalose

card.summary: A protective sugar used in food, eye drops and some skincare; interest is in autophagy research, not proven appearance benefits.
card.note: Autophagy findings come largely from cell and animal models; human trials are small.

quick.overview:
Trehalose is a sugar that many organisms use to survive drying and stress. People encounter it in foods, dry-eye drops and some moisturizers.

Research focuses on neurodegenerative disease and autophagy; no studies were found testing it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: It stabilises proteins and membranes during dehydration. In mammalian cells it has been reported to trigger autophagy, partly through the TFEB pathway, though the mechanism is debated.
quick.risks: It is broken down to glucose by trehalase and is generally treated as safe in foods. Trehalase deficiency is uncommon, and a link to C. difficile outbreaks was disputed by a 2019 study.

lead: Trehalose is a non-reducing disaccharide made of two glucose units joined by an alpha,alpha-1,1 glycosidic bond. It occurs in bacteria, yeast, fungi, insects, invertebrates and plants but cannot be synthesised by vertebrates [1][2].

People encounter it mainly in three appearance-adjacent roles. In skincare, Grokipedia's AI-generated entry reports use as a moisturizing and protective ingredient. In eye care, a 3 percent ophthalmic solution and trehalose-with-hyaluronic-acid artificial tears are used for dry eye, which supports a comfortable, clear-looking eye surface. In dental care, trehalose powder has been used in air-polishing devices that clean biofilm from teeth [1][2][8][14].

Commercially it is also used in food as a mildly sweet stabiliser (about 45 percent as sweet as sucrose) and in biopharmaceutical formulations [1][2]. Research interest centres on its induction of autophagy in neurodegeneration models; small human trials are registered, and no study found tests it for skin or hair appearance [3][12]. Wikipedia also records a disputed link between dietary trehalose and Clostridioides difficile outbreaks, and a 2021 FDA fast-track designation for an injectable form under investigation for spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 [1].

chain: Sugar that protects cell membranes during drying is added to skincare or eye drops
Water is held at the surface and the surface is protected from drying and oxidative injury
Softer, hydrated-looking skin and a more comfortable, clearer eye surface
angle.text: Trehalose is used as a moisture-protecting ingredient because organisms rely on it to survive drying. In people it appears in dry-eye drops and, per one encyclopedia entry, in moisturizers; its benefit for skin appearance has not been tested in published trials.

paras: The glycosidic bond makes trehalose highly resistant to acid hydrolysis and means its closed structure does not glycate proteins [1]. Anhydrous trehalose melts at 203 degrees Celsius, the dihydrate at 97, and solubility in water is about 68.9 g per 100 g at 20 degrees [1]. The dihydrate carries about 90 percent of the calories of sucrose [1].

In many organisms it protects cells during drying and extreme conditions (anhydrobiosis), proposed to act by vitrification or by replacing water around membranes and proteins [1][5]. Insects use it as their main flight fuel and blood sugar [1]. In humans it is split into glucose by the intestinal enzyme trehalase, and it causes a smaller blood-sugar spike than glucose; trehalase deficiency is uncommon but reported in about 10 to 15 percent of Greenlandic Inuit [1]. Industrially it can be derived from corn starch, and five biosynthesis pathways had been reported by 2006, the most common being the TPS/TPP pathway [1].

sections.h: Anhydrobiosis: why it is called a protective sugar
paras: Many bacteria, fungi, plants and invertebrates make trehalose to survive freezing and drying, a state known as anhydrobiosis or cryptobiosis. Two explanations are discussed: vitrification, in which trehalose forms a glassy matrix that prevents ice formation and damage, and water replacement, in which trehalose takes the place of water around membranes and proteins [1][5]. The resurrection plant Selaginella can revive after drying, and tardigrades are reported to carry trehalase genes [1]. Trehalose also stabilises nucleic acids and plays a role in bacterial stress responses, and a 2003 review in Glycobiology describes it as a multifunctional molecule [1][4].

This protective behaviour is the basis for its use as a moisture-retaining and cell-protective ingredient in skincare and eye drops: the idea is that a sugar which shields cells from desiccation in nature can do something similar at the surface of skin or the eye [2][13]. In the eye, a 2019 review reports that trehalose reduced cell apoptosis and oxidative and inflammatory activity at the ocular surface in dry-eye models [13].

H.A.L. Wiggers found trehalose in ergot of rye in 1832, and in 1859 Marcellin Berthelot isolated it from trehala manna and named it [1]. A 2007 paper reported it as an mTOR-independent autophagy enhancer, and 2017 work showed it induces autophagy through TFEB [1][3]. In 2021 the FDA accepted an investigational new drug application and granted fast track status for an injectable form, SLS-005, for spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 [1].

A 2007 Journal of Biological Chemistry paper described trehalose as an mTOR-independent autophagy enhancer that sped the clearance of mutant huntingtin and alpha-synuclein in cell and mouse models [3]. A 2017 study reported that it induces autophagy through TFEB, a master regulator of the autophagy-lysosome pathway, although Wikipedia notes the mechanism is debated [1]. Trehalose has since been investigated, mostly in small registered trials, for spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, Parkinson disease, Alzheimer disease and other conditions (see Clinical studies) [6][7][12][15].
In 2021 the FDA accepted an investigational new drug application and granted fast track status to an injectable trehalose product, SLS-005, for spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 [1].

Grokipedia's AI-generated entry reports trehalose as a moisturizing and protective ingredient in cosmetics, consistent with its biological role in protecting cells from desiccation [2][5]. Wikipedia does not cover cosmetic use [1]. People who care about skin hydration may therefore see it on ingredient lists, usually alongside humectants such as hyaluronic acid.

A 2019 review described trehalose as a non-toxic bioactive sugar that protects cells from oxidative injury and desiccation; in dry eye disease it reduced cell apoptosis and oxidative, inflammatory and proteolytic activity at the ocular surface, and in UVB-irradiated cornea it suppressed photodamage [13]. A 2020 review in Biomolecules also covers trehalose for ocular surface health [14]. A 2023 randomized trial compared trehalose oral spray with carboxymethylcellulose for relieving radiation-induced dry mouth in head and neck cancer patients [11].

A 2022 BMC Oral Health randomized split-mouth trial in 44 participants compared subgingival air polishing with trehalose powder against sonic scaling for biofilm removal in deeper periodontal pockets during supportive periodontal therapy [8].

In food it is used in frozen products such as ice cream because it lowers the freezing point [1]. It is an ingredient, with hyaluronic acid, in an artificial tears product for dry eye [1]. A 2021 trial examined injection-site pain of formulation matrices, which include sugars such as trehalose used as excipients, and a review of commercial antibody formulations covers its use as a stabiliser [9][10].

No studies found testing trehalose for appearance, skin or hair outcomes. Registered and published human studies address other conditions: spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, including a 13-person completed study, a 20-person study and an interim analysis of a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial [6][12]; Parkinson disease [7]; Alzheimer disease [15]; bipolar depression (a 60-person phase 3 trial) [16]; non-alcoholic fatty liver (a 39-person, 12-week study) [17]; acute coronary syndrome [18]; and dry eye [19]. Several are small, have unknown status, were withdrawn, or have no published results.
Laboratory work includes the 2007 cell and mouse study of autophagy and clearance of mutant huntingtin and alpha-synuclein [3].

Earlier reports linked dietary trehalose to Clostridioides difficile outbreaks, but a 2019 study disputed the association [1]. The 2019 ophthalmology review describes trehalose as non-toxic and suitable for extended administration in humans [13].

Outbreaks of epidemic Clostridioides difficile were linked to dietary trehalose after its approval as a food additive widened its use. In January 2018, Francis Collins wrote a blog post on the question and Jimmy Ballard wrote a Nature commentary on it, and a 2018 Nature study by J. Collins and colleagues reported that dietary trehalose enhances virulence of epidemic strains [1]. In 2019, David Eyre and colleagues disputed this, finding that trehalose-metabolism variants were common and were not linked to worse patient outcomes [1]. Wikipedia presents the question as disputed rather than settled [1].

On T Nation, trehalose appears occasionally in carbohydrate discussions: a 2006 poster asked whether trehalose and waxy maize starch could be alternatives to dextrose and maltodextrin, a 2013 poster who had just bought a batch to experiment with described it as less sweet than sugar with a lower glycemic index, and a recovery-supplement ingredient list included a trehalose and oat fibre carbohydrate blend [20][21][22].

claims.claim: Trehalose is a lower-glycemic alternative to dextrose or maltodextrin
claims.believers: A T Nation poster described it as less sweet than sugar with a lower glycemic index, and another asked about it as an alternative to dextrose and maltodextrin [20][21].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says trehalose causes a smaller blood-sugar spike than glucose and carries about 90 percent of the calories of sucrose; no trial in athletes was found [1].

claims.claim: Trehalose hydrates and protects skin like it protects drying organisms
claims.believers: Cosmetic-ingredient descriptions present trehalose as a moisturizing, protective sugar because organisms rely on it to survive desiccation [2][5].
claims.experts: Wikipedia does not cover cosmetic use, and no published trial found tests trehalose for skin appearance; the anhydrobiosis research concerns cells and organisms [1][5].

claims.believers: Artificial-tear products combine trehalose with hyaluronic acid and a 3 percent ophthalmic solution is registered for study [1][19].
claims.experts: A 2019 review describes protective effects on ocular surface cells in lab and clinical contexts, and a 2020 review covers trehalose for ocular surface health [13][14].

claims.claim: Trehalose induces autophagy and may protect against neurodegeneration
claims.believers: Researchers and supplement-minded readers cite the 2007 autophagy findings as the reason for interest in trehalose [3].
claims.experts: The 2007 and 2017 findings come from cell and animal models, human trials are small, and the mechanism is described as debated [1][3][12].

claims.claim: Dietary trehalose fuelled C. difficile outbreaks
claims.believers: The 2018 Nature study reported enhanced virulence of epidemic strains with trehalose [1].
claims.experts: A 2019 analysis by Eyre and colleagues found trehalose-metabolism variants common and unrelated to worse outcomes [1].
